newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: N.Korea says arrests U.S. spy working for South.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea says arrests U.S. spy working for South.

text.p: North Korea said on Sunday it had arrested a U.S. citizen as a spy working for South Korea, dragging Washington further into escalating tensions on the Korean peninsula.
The Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said Evan Carl Hunzike was arrested on August 24 by a North Korean security organisation after he crossed the Amnok River on the China border into North Korea.
KCNA did not identify him further and officials in Seoul and Washington were not immediately available for comment.

"He admitted that he is a U.S. citizen and that he illegally entered the DPRK (Democratic People's Republic of Korea) for the purpose of getting information on its domestic situation," the communique said.

"It has been proved by investigation that he was sent for espionage by South Korea's Agency for National Security planning. He will have to take appropriate penal responsibility under the DPRK criminal law."
The spy allegation drags Washington into an angry feud between North and South Korea over the deaths of 22 of the 26 North Koreans who landed by submarine in the South last month.
The United States maintains 37,000 troops in South Korea to help guarantee a ceasefire that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
Pyongyang has demanded the return of the submarine along with the survivors and the bodies of the dead crew.
On Saturday, North Korea warned of "merciless retaliation" and vowed "blood for blood" in a KCNA communique that also raised espionage charges against Washington.

"It is widely known to the world that the U.S., hand in glove with the puppets, has conducted information-gathering and subversive activities and smear campaign against (North Korea)," the report said.

Washington has been urging calm on both sides, fearing the tension could spiral out of control. Its role in the submarine drama so far has been limited to helping in the hunt for fugitive North Koreans from the vessel.
Analysts said the spy charges appeared to be part of efforts by Pyongyang to divert attention from the submarine incident by creating a new crisis.
North Korea is constantly seeking ways to drive a wedge between Washington and Seoul and engage the United States in direct negotiations.
A crisis over North Korea's suspected nuclear weapons programme was averted by a 1994 deal between the United States and North Korea.

In response to Pyongyang's threats, Seoul has stepped up security at airports, ports and diplomatic missions, assigned more bodyguards to key public figures and tightened vigilance on five west coast islands seen vulnerable to attack.
On Saturday, Seoul's Foreign Ministry warned South Korean travellers to watch out for North Korean terrorism, especially in China and Russia.
"We recommended travel agencies refrain from sending travellers to the northeastern provinces of China and the Far Eastern region of Russia," the ministry said in a statement.
The brutal murder of a South Korean diplomat in the Russian Far East city of Vladivostok last Tuesday sparked fears that the North had begun to make good on its retaliation threats.
Pyongyang has denied involvement in the murder.
Local media reported on Sunday that Seoul would freeze all economic cooperation with the North until ties improved.

The Dong-A Ilbo newspaper quoted the Unification Ministry as saying it would indefinitely delay examining applications by 14 Seoul companies to conduct business in North Korea. Government officials were unavailable to confirm the report.
Tension between North and South Korea, which remain technically at war since their 1950-53 conflict ended only with a truce, has sent the local stock market into a tailspin.
